title: Building the quantum-AI future with Hartmut Neven and James Manyika
transcriptText:
[MUSIC PLAYING]
[WAVES CRASHING]
[ANIMAL CRIES]
[APPLAUSE]
JAMES MANYIKA: Good
morning and thank you
for coming to this
session this morning.
My name is James Manyika.
I'm the President for Research
Labs, Technology & Society
at Google and Alphabet.
And, Google has an
incredible track record
in history of pursuing
very ambitious problems
and challenges and moonshots.
Some could argue
that, in fact, Search
itself is a moonshot,
has been a moonshot.
The work in AI arguably
has been a moonshot.
Some of the earliest
examples of this at Google
were back in 2001,
when Google started
to do things like
auto correction using
machine learning.
And then you could also think
about the work on Waymo,
driverless cars, has
been a moonshot that's
now turned to reality as
we start to ride Waymos.
Hopefully, you've all done that.
And then quantum is
one of those too.
We've focused on trying to build
the idea of quantum computers
for quite a long time.
And that's what we're
going to spend time
talking about this morning.
I should say that the
foundations on which
we're building quantum
computers go all the way back
to the 1980s, when researchers
at Berkeley, Michel Devoret,
John Martinis, and John Clarke
started to work on this idea
of how do you do
superconductivity?
Because up until that
time, the understanding
was that quantum phenomena
was only observable
at the micro level.
And so the question
is, could you ever
make observations
at the macro level?
So they made these incredible
experiments and breakthroughs
that led to the idea of
circuits you could actually
build at the macroscopic scale.
And that's been the
foundation of how
we think about building
quantum computers.
I should say those
three individuals,
Michel Devoret, John
Martinis and John Clarke,
were awarded the Nobel
Prize in physics last year,
and I'm actually glad
to say two of them,
Michel Devoret
and John Martinis,
have actually been part of
our quantum team at Google.
Well, John Martinis is no longer
with us at the quantum team,
but Michel Devoret is actually
our Chief Hardware Scientist
on the quantum computing
team at Google.
I'm going to be joined in this
conversation by Hartmut Neven.
Hartmut is the leader and
founder of our Quantum AI team.
[APPLAUSE]
Take a seat.
HARTMUT NEVEN: Hey.
JAMES MANYIKA: Hartmut founded
this team back in 2012, the idea
how can we build and achieve
this moonshot of building
quantum computers.
So he and I are going
to have a conversation.
We work together.
So this is always a pleasure
for me to chat with Hartmut.
And we'll talk about first
of what quantum computing is;
where we are, what
progress are we making;
and what are some
of the challenges,
opportunities, and things
that we're excited about;
and what can we look forward to.
So Hartmut, thanks
for joining me.
HARTMUT NEVEN: Oh, a pleasure.
Thanks, everyone, for coming.
JAMES MANYIKA: Well let's start.
Quantum computing
or quantum mechanics
is one of these
very complex topics.
How would you describe
quantum computing?
Give us some basics.
What are some of
the basic things
that one would
have to understand
about quantum computing?
HARTMUT NEVEN: So if
you want to understand
where the superpower of
quantum computers comes from,
the one concept we need to grasp
is the concept of superposition.
So let me give you a quick
quantum computing 101
and explain to you
what superposition is.
Essentially, quantum
physics states
that any system
can simultaneously
exist in many configurations.
That's what is called
a superposition.
So to help you visualize
it as the following.
Let's look at the system
we are forming here right
now in the room.
And we are sitting here in
one specific configuration.
But you can easily envision
another one, like the two of you
could switch seats.
You, James and I, we
could switch seats.
So there are other
configurations.
But a reading of
quantum physics would
suggest that all these or
many of these constellations,
configurations, are
realized right now,
and they evolve
together in time.
And that is what we take
advantage of in our chips.
JAMES MANYIKA: But I think
one of the things that often,
so how would you describe
because we go from--
we can try to build physical
qubits and then logical qubits.
Explain the idea of
qubits, and how should we
think about that, what that is?
HARTMUT NEVEN: So a qubit
is short for quantum bit.
And it's essentially
a bit or qubits
are a number of bits that I
can put into superposition.
So I will later show you, or
maybe we do this right now.
I show you a chip
that contains qubits.
I'm not sure the
camera can see this.
So this is a Willow chip,
one of our more recent chips.
And it has 105 qubits in there.
And now that you know
what a superposition is,
you can envision the following.
Those qubits can be in
a superposition state.
So a single
configuration for 105
qubits it's just a
string of zeros and ones.
We call it a bit
string of length 105.
But similar, as we
envisioned before,
you can just flip a few qubits
and you get a different bit
string.
You flip a few more, you
get a different bit string.
How many bit strings
can there be?
I say 105 quantum bits in this
chip is 2 to the power of 105.
And then, as amazing as this
may sound, in just one clock
cycle of this chip, we can touch
2 to the 105 different objects,
2 to the 105 different strings.
That is an enormous number.
And therefore, you arrive
at these situations
where this tiny chip can
do certain computations
that the largest factory-sized
data center would
need an inordinate amount of
time, 10 septillion years,
in a recent demonstration.
JAMES MANYIKA: In my opening--
[APPLAUSE]
Thank you.
In my opening remarks, I
mentioned the idea that
we're building on breakthroughs
that our colleagues,
Michel Devoret and
others made in the 1980s.
And one of the key things
that they worked on
was this idea of
superconductivity
as a way with the
ideas of how do you do,
if you like, quantum tunneling
with Josephson circuits,
to be able to do
superconductivity.
That often requires that we
actually cool these things down
to a few degrees above Kelvin.
And so in the lab,
describe the fact
that you're actually building
these extraordinary fridges
so you can cool things down to
a few degrees above 0 Kelvin.
Why are we building it that way?
How does that work?
HARTMUT NEVEN: So the different
ways how you can make qubits,
in quantum mechanics,
famously, you
might think of quantum mechanics
as a physics of the very small,
the thing that describes
electrons, atoms.
But this is actually incorrect.
Quantum physics is the law
of the land at all scales,
at the microscopic, all the
way to the universe as a whole.
It just happens to be the case
that quantum effects can easily
be controlled, managed, and
observed on microscopic scales.
So a natural choice to
build a qubit, therefore,
would be to just use an
atom, to use, let's say,
the states of a spin of an
electron or of a nucleus.
But these things are tiny
and hard to engineer with.
So the ingenious inventions
that got the Nobel Prize,
as you explained, was
to essentially make
macroscopic qubits.
So using a loop of
superconducting wires,
you can have the same property
of quantized energy levels
and other hallmark
features of atoms.
You can have this at
a macroscopic scale,
much easier to put into
a chip and work with.
JAMES MANYIKA: Yeah, and
in fact, one of the things
that you always like
to say, Hartmut,
is that your lab is probably
the coldest place in our galaxy.
Can you explain that?
HARTMUT NEVEN: Yeah so to work
with these artificial atoms that
are made out of
superconducting material,
and many of you may
know that right now,
to get superconductivity, a
macroscopic quantum effect,
you have to cool down the
metals or the materials
to a very low degree.
So we work currently
with aluminum qubits.
You could have used
niobium, tantalum.
There are some choices.
But all of them have to
go down to about 1 Kelvin.
So that's pretty cool.
But we don't stop there.
We go even further down
to just 10 millikelvin
because temperature is really
the physicists' term for noise.
And we don't want to have noise
in our chips, so the colder
we can make it, the better.
JAMES MANYIKA: So
talk a little bit
about what's difficult about
building quantum computers.
What are some of
the key challenges
you have to solve if you're
trying to build these systems?
HARTMUT NEVEN: So in
the very beginning,
I explained to you that the
key ingredients, a key resource
is superposition states.
And we need to keep
these superpositions
of different
constellations alive.
And the times that measured,
there's an important time.
We call it the coherence
time of a quantum computer.
It essentially measures how long
these superpositions survive.
And you want to make this
the longer the better.
And initially, we
all thought, oh, this
is a key battle to fight,
the key engineering
challenge to get right.
But it turned out in this
area we made rapid progress.
We went from 20 microsecond
coherence time to 10 times more,
now over 250 microseconds,
pretty much enough
for what we need for use
for quantum computing.
So it's not the key
physics challenge anymore.
It's more mundane system-level
issues that hold us back.
JAMES MANYIKA: So why
would anybody want
to build a quantum computer?
What are some of the useful
applications, assuming
we get there?
We'll talk a little bit in a
little while about where we are.
But why would you want
a quantum computer?
HARTMUT NEVEN: Yeah, so
on the application side,
there are various areas.
One thing that's important for
the audience to understand,
quantum computers,
as far as we know,
will always be a
specialist tool.
It will be very good for
certain applications,
not so useful for others.
So what are some of the useful
applications we can think of?
The first one is we call it
Richard Feynman's killer app.
Feynman was the
first one to realize
that if you want to simulate a
system where quantum effects are
important, you run against
this combinatorial challenge.
That is you have to consider all
these different constellations,
and that's just impossibly hard
for classical computers to do.
So he coined, you saw
it in the initial video,
that if you want to make a
faithful simulation of nature,
you better make it
quantum mechanical.
JAMES MANYIKA: But I think often
when people think about quantum
computers, we often think
about the speed-up benefits,
that it will be able to
run things much faster.
But also there are
some problems that
are inherently quantum
that you can only work on.
So can you make a distinction
between where are we
mostly capsulizing just on
speed-ups versus when we're
actually working on things
that can only be worked on
with quantum computers?
HARTMUT NEVEN: Yeah.
Let's say a few examples.
I just gave you this
general overview,
Richard Feynman's killer
app, the simulation
of quantum systems.
That is actually a task that is
necessary more often than you
might think.
Let's pick a nice one.
Batteries, sounds a
little bit boring,
but we would all
feel so much better
if we could fly in an airplane
that is powered by batteries,
not by kerosene
when we do vacation.
So now there are things like
lithium air batteries, which,
they have a higher energy
density than kerosene.
So you could perfectly do that.
Unfortunately, they
are very brittle.
They have various
material science issues.
So that's why we
don't use them today.
But a quantum computer
would be a marvelous tool
to simulate various designs
for lithium air batteries.
And then we can have some not
just in cars, but in airplanes
too.
JAMES MANYIKA: Right, yeah.
Maybe you can correct me,
I think there's currently
something like 70-plus kind of
algorithms and problems that
people in the community have
actually identified as things
where a quantum computer would
be the most useful way to tackle
those problems.
Is this still 70, or
is that list growing?
HARTMUT NEVEN: Yeah.
Thank you for
mentioning this number.
I should have checked
up on the website
because when we started
talking it was like 60.
Now it's 70.
And I hope that in
a few years, there
will be 600 or 700 important, 10
times more, important algorithms
where quantum computers give
you a decisive advantage.
JAMES MANYIKA: Right.
So Hartmut, let's talk about
where we are at this stage.
I mean, I remember
when you and I first
started working together,
I guess five years ago,
you had a roadmap which
had six milestones.
First of all, can you
describe the roadmap
you've had for progress towards
building a quantum computer,
and where are we
on that roadmap?
What progress are we making?
HARTMUT NEVEN: So
originally, and if anybody
has watched the work of
the Google Quantum AI team,
you may have seen we typically
show it first thing whenever
we give a talk or
presentation is our mission
is to build a useful quantum
computer for otherwise
unsolvable problems.
To get to that, we had set out
a roadmap with six milestones
to build such a machine.
And the first two milestones
we cleared a few years ago.
So our very first
one was in 2019,
where we showed
for the first time
that a quantum computer could
compute something quickly
in minutes that would have
taken many, many years
on a classical
supercomputer to do.
So that was milestone one.
And milestone two was there is
a technique called quantum error
correction.
That is essentially
the technology
you need to keep those
superposition states alive.
And that was understood in
theory well since the '90s.
But then, in '22,
for the first time,
we reduced this to practice
and built a machine
where quantum error correction
successfully reduced the errors
in a machine in practice.
And we are now
ahead of, hopefully
fingers crossed, we
solve it later this year
as milestone three.
This would be one
very good module out
of which you can build a large
modular quantum computer.
JAMES MANYIKA:
And so by the time
we get to hopefully milestone
five or six, hopefully
we'll have useful applications.
But let's talk a
little bit about some
of the recent breakthroughs.
I mean you showed
the Willow chip.
This is a chip we showed
the world back in 2024.
And I think there are two
key breakthroughs associated
with that.
One is the fact that it was
able to do in a few minutes what
would take the world's
fastest supercomputer 10
septillion years.
That's 1 with 25 zeros next
to which is extraordinary.
But the other one, in some ways
more important demonstration,
was this idea of below
threshold error correction.
Can you explain what that is
and why that matters so much?
HARTMUT NEVEN: Yeah, so
quantum error correction
is a technology you need to
keep the important superposition
states alive.
And for the very
first time, as I said,
we cleared that hurdle in '22.
But the community
wasn't too impressed
because the errors just
came down by a few percent.
And people said, well,
even though before--
so how do you do
error correction?
Typically, you use redundancy.
That's what we
use in engineering
to make things safer.
So you take a number
of physical qubits,
as we call them, to
orchestrate them into one
more stable logical qubit.
That is what error
correction does.
And then when we try--
before when people tried it
they introduced more redundancy.
But there was more stuff.
Now more qubits, more wires,
more measurement devices.
So the error always came
down, or sorry the opposite,
the error went up.
And then in '22, we made it
come down for the first time,
but an unimpressive few percent.
And then with Willow,
we just redid this.
And in '24, we basically did
the same experiment again.
But now it was already
much higher quality chip.
And the error came
down by a factor of 2.
And then the field
for the first time
was, oh, this seems to
really work for good.
JAMES MANYIKA: Right.
So that was an
important breakthrough.
And then last year, we had
another big breakthrough.
But maybe to set up
that breakthrough,
all these typical
benchmarks we've been using,
such as the 10 septillion
years and so forth, we're
talking about using a
particular benchmark mechanism
called random circuit
sampling as a way to measure,
but it's not a very
useful computation.
But it's useful to
measure progress.
But the breakthrough last year
with Quantum Echoes was actually
the first time anybody, I think,
had shown a useful algorithm.
Can you talk about
Quantum Echoes
and why that breakthrough
was important?
HARTMUT NEVEN: Yes.
So you said it nicely.
So the initial demonstrations
that quantum chips
can do something
impressive was done
on exotic mathematical
benchmarks where
essentially problems that you
or people in the real world
don't have, good
for benchmarking.
And then the criticism
was show us something
that I would care for.
And Quantum Echoes was
the answer to this.
It was the first
quantum algorithm
that can do a useful task.
JAMES MANYIKA: Talk
about the task.
Because we had a demonstration
where we worked with researchers
at Berkeley and others
to actually show
a useful use of Quantum Echoes.
Can you describe that work?
HARTMUT NEVEN: Yeah, so
Quantum Echoes is essentially
the quintessential quantum
machine learning algorithm.
It allows you to learn from
readily available data.
It's data that comes from
nuclear magnetic resonance
imaging, so in NMR machines that
pharmaceutical companies use.
Or if you go to a hospital
and do an MRI scan,
that's also nuclear
magnetic resonance imaging.
So to get out of these
devices more information,
that's where the Quantum
Echoes algorithm applies.
JAMES MANYIKA: And I
think in that example,
what you were able
to observe was
to show that, for
the first time,
you were able to
measure these kind
of dihedral angles of these very
hard to understand molecules.
I think, was it a benzene,
a couple benzene molecules?
Can you--
HARTMUT NEVEN: Yeah, we then--
and typically when you
have such new algorithms,
there are a few steps to
really lodge it in practice.
So initially, we
showed it on some proof
of principle problems.
And then you go closer to
what chemists care for.
So there was it's
called a diphenyl.
It has two benzene rings.
And chemists didn't know how are
these two rings rotated relative
to each other.
So we computed this angle
using Quantum Echoes.
And showed, look, you can answer
real open questions in chemistry
with that algorithm.
JAMES MANYIKA:
One of the things,
I mean so the quantum
team at Google
is actually called Quantum AI.
And we should talk about
that, why that name.
And there's always
a question about,
so do these two things
need each other.
Does quantum computing
need AI and does
AI need quantum computer?
Can you explain the origin
of the name Quantum AI
for the team?
And then I'd love
to maybe debate
you a little bit on this
question of AI and quantum.
Why that name?
HARTMUT NEVEN: So yeah, why
is our team called Quantum AI?
And that was-- actually I worked
in AI for most of my career.
I actually here is
self-driving cars.
My PhD was on self-driving cars.
I joined Google doing computer
vision, visual search.
But at the time, it dawned on
me that real, powerful future AI
wants to have access to
the most potent, capable
computational substrate
we can think of,
and currently that
is quantum computing.
So I thought
quantum AI should be
able to do tasks that AI
running on classical machines
will never be able to do.
And then in 2012, we set
out, based on the thesis,
to show that this
is really true.
JAMES MANYIKA: And I think
one of the reasons, one
of the contributions that
quantum computing can make to AI
is in particular data sets.
HARTMUT NEVEN: Yeah.
So maybe we should
advertise this, James.
So for those of you who
want to know more details,
there will be a special issue
of "Daedalus" coming out.
You're the editor.
And there we put an essay that
is called "Quantum Plus AI
Equals Quantum AI," and it
speaks about this bidirectional
acceleration.
How do we use AI today
to accelerate progress
in quantum computing, and how
starting now, and even more so
in the future, quantum resources
will help solve novel tasks?
JAMES MANYIKA: Yeah and I think
one of those examples, which
is incredible to
see was how there
was a deep collaboration
between the DeepMind team
and the quantum team around
this idea of alpha qubits
as a way to think about how
to use AI and machine learning
techniques to actually help
the progress we've been making
on error correction.
There was one example where AI
was actually benefiting quantum.
Have there been other
examples like that?
HARTMUT NEVEN: Yeah, let me give
you also your previous question
I haven't properly answered yet.
So how can quantum help AI?
There are probably a
dozen different ways.
Let me give you one
or two examples.
So AlphaFold, a
resounding success,
used in labs all over the world.
To train AlphaFold, we needed
data sets that started to be
collected in the 1970s.
It took 50 years to make things
like the protein database
to train AlphaFold, very
painstaking work by many PhDs,
lots of government grants.
So a quantum computer
would be able to produce
very valuable training
sets in many settings
where it's difficult to make
those training sets otherwise.
So we expect this to be the very
first contribution of quantum
to AI that we say, look,
here's a great data set
that you should use.
And actually, as a
late-breaking piece of news,
just last week, we had first
data sets relevant to material
science where we
thought, oh wow,
they have the
quality good enough.
We should ship them to our
colleagues at DeepMind.
JAMES MANYIKA: That's fantastic.
One of the things that I
find pretty exciting about,
even though, of course, we're
on this moonshot journey
to build a fully error-corrected
quantum computer,
there's a lot of great
science and discovery
that's actually
happening along the way.
Can you give a
couple of examples?
I mean, one of my favorite ones
was the holographic effect,
which goes back to something,
a conjecture that Einstein had.
But talk a little bit
about some of the examples
of the incredible
science you and the team
are able to do along the way.
HARTMUT NEVEN: So now that we
have chips with a few hundred
qubits, we can make good
on Richard Feynman's dream
and simulate quantum systems
and study their properties
and learn new things.
And you mentioned already a few.
There is one very
exotic one which
created quite the firestorm
in the scientific community.
And it will be hard to explain
fully the science behind it.
You might have heard of the
effect of quantum entanglement
that two quantum particles can
be correlated at long distances.
You may also have
heard about wormholes,
which is a connection through
space between two distant space
points.
And there is a field in physics.
It's called holographic duality
that claims that these two
processes are the same.
So if that is
really true, then we
can use entangled qubits,
which we can produce
on our chip to make wormholes.
And we essentially
created a wormhole.
And I use the word
created not simulated.
Because strictly speaking,
if the holograph,
if the string
theorists are right
and this duality exists,
then it was actually a tiny--
don't worry, you
wouldn't have fallen
in-- but a tiny wormhole
was actually created.
JAMES MANYIKA: Yeah, I
mean, this gets very exotic
pretty quickly.
I mean, you've also been doing
experiments on quantum gravity
as well.
And you've also been doing even
understanding deeper questions
about electromagnetism that we
didn't fully understand before.
So there's a lot of incredible
science going on along the way.
HARTMUT NEVEN: Yeah, so
one thing we are proud of
is that there is our team
produces this string,
dense string of
high-impact publications
that discusses exactly
that, that discoveries made
through this process,
quantum simulation
of interesting systems.
And others, just
the names, we won't
explain, but time crystals.
We made time crystals.
That's the closest you
get, that physics lets
you get to perpetual mobile.
It's essentially a system
that stays in periodic motion
forever, without needing
to exchange any energy
with the environment.
Or another exotic thing
was non-abelian anyons.
I know that's a mouthful.
What is that?
But it's something also goes
seemingly against common sense.
It's essentially the
situation, imagine
you build a little house
out of LEGO blocks.
And there are, let's say, two
bricks that look the same,
and you switch them out and
you look again at your house,
because they were the same,
nothing should have changed.
But in quantum physics,
there was a prediction
that this may be different.
That even though you swap
two identical particles,
the overall system
changes properties.
And that we showed in practice
that really, yes, that exists.
JAMES MANYIKA: Often when
people think a lot about quantum
computing, I mean,
you and I can talk
about all these extraordinary
applications in biology
and chemistry, in
materials and so forth.
But I think the one
application or use
that most people think
about is encryption.
Ever since, for example,
Shor's algorithm,
the idea that most of our
cryptographic encryption systems
rely on the fact that these
are incredibly hard problems
for classical
computers to solve.
And so therefore, we rely on the
difficulty of those computations
as a way to think about
our encryption systems.
But if you had a
quantum computer,
you probably could
crack those systems.
And so recently, you made
and the team made some news
recently, to suggest
that, in fact, the ability
to build systems that can
crack RSA encryption and also
elliptic curve cryptography
systems is not that far away.
Can you talk a little bit
about what the news was
and what the progress
has been on building
those kinds of systems?
HARTMUT NEVEN: Yeah
so fortunately,
many of the natural applications
for quantum computers
are these very human-kind
friendly things,
like design drugs
quicker, better batteries,
fusion reactors, and many
important humankind challenges.
But one of the more
problematic applications
of quantum computing
is it can be very
powerful for crypto analysis.
And indeed, in
quantum computing,
it's not just that the
hardware has made progress.
It's also the algorithms
have made progress.
So we were able to show that
you need less and less resources
to do the simulations,
but also cryptoanalysis,
and therefore indeed the
timelines are moving inward.
It's not that you can wait
till late 2030s before you have
to worry about it.
Actually, Google put a
blog post out saying,
hey, we need to move to more
powerful post-quantum crypto
schemes already by 2029.
JAMES MANYIKA: Yeah, maybe to
put this in concrete terms,
I think back in 2019, I think
the view in the field was that
if you wanted a quantum system
that was capable of cracking RSA
